title: Kimi Antonelli takes statement pole for the Monaco GP
content:
Kimi Antonelli secured pole position for the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix, beating Max Verstappen by 0.043-seconds. It will be an all-Ferrari second row, with Lewis Hamilton lining up third and Charles Leclerc fourth.

Saturday is when the magic of Monaco comes alive. Race day usually faces criticism because the tight confines of the street circuit combined with the larger size of the modern day Formula 1 cars means there’s a lack of overtaking.

Qualifying on Saturday, though, is a thrill, as the 22 drivers navigate through the streets of the principality where there’s little room for error.

Antonelli, who has won the last four consecutive races, held provisional pole after the initial runs in Q3, but Verstappen was just 0.001-seconds off at this stage. Ferrari driver Hamilton held provisional third but was nearly two-tenths of a second off of Antonelli.

The only one who didn’t have a representative time was Leclerc, who made a mistake at Massenet. But his subsequent run looked much closer to what you’d expect from the Monaco native. He looked lightning quick and pipped Antonelli’s provisional pole lap by 0.024-seconds.

But it wasn’t enough. Verstappen, Hamilton and Antonelli all put together final laps that were quicker again, and Leclerc then smacked the wall at Tabac on his final lap.

This marks Antonelli’s fourth pole position of the season and likely will be another confidence boost for the 19-year-old, especially as his title rival — George Russell in the other Mercedes — only ended up sixth and lacked pace throughout qualifying.

After climbing from his Mercedes, Antonelli sat in the middle of the red sofa inside the Monaco news conference room — taking deep breaths as he waited for Verstappen and Hamilton to join him.

He commented before the microphones were turned on — and later said on the record — that he was still a bit shaky after producing that stunning pole lap.

“It’s just super intense,” the Italian said. “You have no margin (for) mistakes. And when it’s about polishing those last two, three tenths, it’s never easy.”

Looking back on his lap, Antonelli felt he “put everything together.” He noted how the beginning of the session was more difficult than he anticipated, adding that “the track felt a little bit weird” and “the car felt a little bit more oversteer-y than FP3.”

But as the laps passed in qualifying, the car started coming together more for Antonelli. That growing confidence was evident in the 19-year-old.

Monaco is a unique situation where qualifying matters significantly more than the grand prix. But Antonelli has struggled with starts this season, sometimes losing multiple positions heading into Turn 1. Given how this race can become a procession, he needs to nail it when the lights go out on Sunday afternoon.

In the same news conference, Hamilton and Verstappen were asked whether they had any advice for Antonelli regarding his starts.

The Dutchman turned to him and said, “So, when the lights go, you wait one second.” Laughter echoed throughout the room. Hamilton chimed in with “two seconds” instead.

While the cars are a bit smaller and lighter compared to last season, it still looks like it’ll be a tight squeeze if someone attempts a pass on Sunday. In the Formula 3 on Saturday, a collision occurred at the hairpin when Trident driver Freddie Slater tried to make a move, taking out two other cars.

The Monaco GP will be a bit different compared to other races this season, as the drivers are able to go flat out and do not have to manage their engine energy levels as they have to do elsewhere, because the many braking zones and lack of long straights in Monaco means their energy levels remain high around the lap.

But the top three on Saturday still anticipate overtaking will be difficult on Sunday. Verstappen pointed out the difficulty of overtaking in the junior category races held so far this weekend.

Meanwhile, Antonelli said, “Unless I wait for one second (at the start) or unless you do a big mistake, I think it’s very difficult (for anyone to pass).”
